title: How Karoline Leavitt Debased Her Job
excerpt: The lie is the elemental matter of the Trump administration
body: The lie is the elemental matter of the Trump administration
The value of lying is Donald Trump’s deepest belief
He built his celebrity image through shameless and constant deceit that permitted him to bounce from blunder to blunder while constantly reeling in new suckers

Lying is also what binds his loyalists to him: The highest calling of any figure in Trump world is to refuse any concessions to reality when Trump commands it, and the surest ticket to oblivion is to speak the truth
All of this has made the job of press secretary in a Trump administration less, not more, important than it normally is
In most administrations, the White House press secretary has a unique role in shaping public opinion, whereas the other staffers are concerned principally with governing
In Trump’s White House, distorting reality, rather than trying to improve it, is the highest priority for every official, including and especially the president himself
In an administration where everybody’s main priority is to lie on television, the role of the press secretary is redundant
Karoline Leavitt, who departed as press secretary this week, did the job perfectly well
But the job, as defined by this administration, is not terribly demanding
Historically, press secretaries engaged in “spin,” a now-antiquated term to describe the delicate art of arranging facts in the most flattering light

Its practitioners must grasp the underlying reality, which points must be danced around and which emphasized, and how to walk a reporter from their skeptical premise to the administration’s desired conclusion
Leavitt never engaged in spin, and she probably wouldn’t know how

Her method of replying to queries relied on the blunt-force repetition of talking points, however unresponsive they might be, sprinkling in heavy doses of personal abuse and slander. [ From the July issue: Use it or lose it ] Consider a sample of her style, plucked somewhat at random
It is the first item on a celebratory list of Leavitt highlights released by the administration—which is to say that it is not some unfortunate slipup but one of her proudest moments
The exchange in question took place on January 15, 2026, between Leavitt and Niall Stanage, the White House columnist for The Hill

Stanage asked Leavitt how to square then–Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem’s statement that the department had done “everything correctly” with the fact that 32 people had died in ICE custody over the past year, 170 U.S. citizens had been detained, and Renee Good had been shot and killed
A few lines of defense sprang to my mind as I listened to the question
If my job were to defend the administration, I’d reply that, yes, 32 people died in custody, but that figure says nothing about whether those deaths were caused by ICE

And don’t all police agencies sometimes detain the wrong person in the course of investigating crimes? If ICE is performing somewhat less efficiently than other law-enforcement agencies, maybe it needs more resources for facilities and training
A handful of facts and figures could have reframed this horrific scandal as a one-off failure amid mere business as usual
She first responded by asking Stanage why he believed that Good had been shot
When Stanage replied that he believed that an agent had acted recklessly, Leavitt savaged him as biased. “You’re a left-wing hack
You’re posing in this room as a journalist
And it’s so clear by the premise of your question,” she said. “You should be reporting on the facts
You should be reporting on the cases.” [ David A

Graham: A dangerous new attack on press freedom ] Despite attacking Stanage for supposedly failing to report on “the facts,” which his question included, Leavitt’s reply did not cite any numbers at all. “Do you have the numbers of how many American citizens were killed at the hands of illegal aliens, who ICE is trying to remove from this country?” she asked, without producing them herself

In the same exchange, Leavitt complained that Stanage had degraded the august profession of White House reporter: “You and the people in the media who have such biases but fake like you’re a journalist—you shouldn’t even be sitting in that seat.” In reality, Leavitt herself, in one of her first and most important moves as press secretary, invited numerous opinion journalists and influencers to hold permanent seats in the briefing room alongside traditional journalists
So even if it actually were true that Stanage is “biased,” her complaint that this would disqualify him from the job would still have been at odds with her policy
This exchange, in miniature, shows how Leavitt conducted her briefings
Instead of the journalists in the room, her audience was loyalists who require no convincing and who believe that any news story that reflects poorly on Trump is by definition a hoax
Leavitt communicated effectively to this audience because she seemed to be one of them

For this reason, she will be easily replaced by another, equally effective functionary plucked from among the millions of Americans capable of the rudimentary task of responding to questions with repetitive, childish insults
In an administration rife with memorable rogues, Leavitt will fade into obscurity.

title: Welcome to the Scrolling Backlash
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube A lot of people are getting tired of their phone—they’re sick of the algorithms and overwhelmed by what can f
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube A lot of people are getting tired of their phone—they’re sick of the algorithms and overwhelmed by what can feel like a loss of control
The Atlantic staff writer Julie Beck dug into why and how people are trying to renegotiate their relationships with technology

She and our colleagues just released a five-part podcast series called How to Touch Grass , and in this episode, Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel talks with Beck about why people are nostalgic for the pre-internet days, how our brains are changing, and the good that can come from getting lost

The following is a transcript of the episode: Charlie Warzel: How does the phone make you feel? How does a TikTok binge make you feel, or even just, like, a before-bed scrolling session that we all have? Julie Beck: Oh, sick
It’s like when the aliens get you, right? They take you up and then they probe you, or they do whatever they do, and then when you come back down, you don’t know what happened
So I feel like I have emerged from lost time and like what happened during that time is unclear, but I don’t feel good
Warzel: I don’t know that I have the amnesia part of it, but it promotes self-loathing in a way that like truly no other activity does because it just feels like a deletion of my one precious life
I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain , a show where today we’re gonna answer a question
Maybe it’s even the question of the online age
How can we live lives where we use tech and don’t let it use us? This is the animating question of How to Touch Grass , a new podcast series by my colleagues here at The Atlantic

Over five episodes, Julie Beck and her co-host and producer, Natalie Brennan, explore what exactly is happening in this moment that has so many of us out there feeling like we need to renegotiate our relationships to our technology
At the beginning of this year, I made a few predictions about trends that we might see, and one of them was that there would be what I was calling a scrolling backlash

That people are just really tired of their phones, of the algorithmic internet, of this idea that they’re being manipulated all the time, and that their attention is being directed towards things that don’t make them feel good or whole or happy
Now, as predictions go, this is a pretty safe one, but it’s really been borne out in recent months
These things are hard to measure, but you can just feel it out there in the world

In the artists who are asking that people leave their phones at home or in their pockets at concerts, in the genuine concern over whether younger generations are going to be able to read like older generations

And while the data-center backlash that we’re seeing right now is complicated, and it’s about a lot of things, including AI, I also see that as an outgrowth of this larger frustration about the role that big tech is playing in our lives and the way that people just feel this fuzzy loss of agency right now
It’s a loss that just can’t be separated from the devices that we use
How to Touch Grass digs into so many of the ideas that I’ve been trying to poke at here in the first year of this podcast
Our motto here at Galaxy Brain is that we pay attention to where we pay attention, which also happens to be exactly what I found so valuable about Julie and Natalie’s work
And so I decided to bring Julie on here today to talk about this moment and to talk about what she’s learned in this series

How badly have our attention spans actually been fractured? How has she reevaluated her relationship to all of her devices? Is the backlash that we’re feeling and seeing right now justified? And crucially, where might we go from here? Julie joins me now to talk about it all. [ Music ] Warzel: Julie, welcome to Galaxy Brain
Let’s talk about the touch-grass moment that I think we are in
Even even the phrase itself, right? Why is “touching grass” something that people are talking about? And what made you want to just dig in and report on it? Beck: Yes
So we had originally thought about calling the season How to Log Off , but that’s not as fun

But I think it also speaks to just a sort of general renegotiation that people are doing right now between how much they actually want to be on their devices and how much they actually want to be inhabiting the embodied world around you and the grass and the trees and the people and everybody around you

We wanted to look at like the various shifts that are happening both in the culture of the internet itself and the technology itself but also the shifts in the culture of how people are thinking about their devices and how they’re talking about them, and how much they want to use them
Warzel: Why did you feel like this was a project you wanted to embark on? Beck: I have deleted and re-downloaded TikTok on my phone roughly four to five times
Beck: And it’s usually like my friend ends up sending me a Lord of the Rings meme and then you click it, and to click it, to see it, you have to re-download the app, and they get me every time
Beck: Lord of the Rings memes are the gateway drug kids

But no, I noticed something happening maybe six-ish months ago when whenever I was on my last round of being on TikTok, which is: Every time I would go on there, I would get nothing but reels of “how to be offline more”, like “how to live more analog,” “how to heal your attention span” on this app where I was actively in the process of degrading my attention span

So I thought that irony was interesting, and so I think there was a shift that I was just sensing within myself, but also in conversations that I would have with people in real life and in what I was seeing online of people really trying to just be on their phones less, be on social media less
And I was curious why now, when obviously we’ve had smartphones for a very long time, we’ve had the internet for a very long time, we’ve had social media for a long time

Warzel: What is the answer to that? Why now? Beck: Why now? I think some of it is that we’ve had it for long enough that the shine’s off the apple, right? And I think some of it is a confluence of these different bigger conversations

Obviously, there’s like a big push by many to get kids off of social media, right? Or there’s lawsuits against Instagram, and What is Instagram doing to our mental health? And so I do think that those things have leaked down in some way, but also even TikTok, right, has been pretty popular for a few years
We’ve had a few years of living in this sort of algorithmically optimized short-form-video environment

And it’s gotten to the point where maybe people have had enough experience with it that they’re starting to see the effects in their own lives and like starting to question that rather than just, Oh, isn’t this fun? I can watch Lord of the Rings memes

And I think combining that with the sort of arrival of AI on the scene, right? And seeing all of these extreme stories about people replacing relationships with AI, using AI as a friend or a lover—God forbid—I think there’s been a sort of opposite, if not equal, reaction to valuing more the embodied world and the real social relationships that we had

So I think people are reacting in part to the sort of evolution of the internet culture and social-media environment and the arrival of this new technology that’s really like getting its little tendrils into every area of our lives

Warzel: So one of the episodes—to pivot here—explores nostalgia, which I think is a very big part of all of this hand-wringing that we are all personally going through, right? Is this moment different from others? Are we doing something uniquely awful to our brains that none of our ancestors ever did? And when you talk about nostalgia, there’s particularly a focus on young people who weren’t really around to have that pre-internet life

title: The Limits of Yayoi Kusama’s Infinity
excerpt: Years before the polka-dotted pumpkins, before the Instagrammable Infinity Mirror Rooms, Yayoi Kusama made art that was charged with oppositional energy
body: Years before the polka-dotted pumpkins, before the Instagrammable Infinity Mirror Rooms, Yayoi Kusama made art that was charged with oppositional energy
Her performances, in which she painted dots onto the naked bodies of her collaborators, were an expression of ’60s counterculture
They were protests against the Vietnam War, rebukes to the art market
Her Accumulations—soft sculptures of furniture or common household items covered in stuffed, handsewn penis shapes—were hilarious critiques of phallocentrism and early examples of feminist art
Kusama was, in other words, part of the artistic avant-garde
Her death, at 97, is a cold reminder that the avant-garde no longer exists
You could point to Andy Warhol, Jeff Koons, Takashi Murakami, or Keith Haring, but in many ways, no one epitomizes the collapse of the avant-garde more vividly than Kusama
It’s very hard not to like her Infinity Mirror Room installations and playful gourds, and not to smile when you see Kusama’s endearing face framed by her signature brightly colored bobbed wig
But at a certain point, you can’t help but feel that she stopped being an artist and chose instead to become a highly profitable brand

In death as in life, her name bestrides a tightly managed, commercially successful global enterprise with diverse revenue streams, including high-profile partnerships with luxury labels, licensed merchandise, and strictly managed intellectual-property protection
Kusama’s large-scale sculptures and immersive installations break attendance records at museums and galleries around the world, and her works regularly set records at auction
In her final years, she was one of the world’s top-selling contemporary artists
Decades before all of that, though, Kusama was a creative maverick
After moving to New York from Tokyo in the late 1950s, she became a pioneer of both pop art and minimalism, then a key figure in performance art
She called her early breakthrough paintings—expansive, swirling fields of tightly packed dots—Infinity Nets

Before even Andy Warhol (although after Marcel Duchamp), she made her own persona an expression of her art, paving the way for such figures as Gilbert and George, the British-artist duo who made life itself a performance
Seymour Wally / NY Daily News / Getty Yayoi Kusama paints Kent Feathergill in 1967
Kusama’s artworks had countercultural energy
They broke down starchy inhibitions and wobbled magnificently on the edge of the rational
They tried, in other words, to open up new ways of seeing
That was what the avant-garde was all about: It was an attempt to see the world afresh

For many of its leading figures, from the Impressionists in the 1870s to conceptual artists a century later, this also meant proposing new and better solutions to the problem of how to be and how to live together

These proposals, many times rooted in sympathy and love, were presented as alternatives to the political structures and market logic that had so often led to war, exploitation, hopelessness, and suffering
Even when attempts to turn these imagined alternatives into reality failed—and often dismally—the avant-garde stood in a clear relationship to modernity’s traumas
It was like the whistle cap in the spout of a boiling kettle: both a release of suppressed pressures (psychic and cultural) and an alarm
But society got sick of hearing the alarm
Kusama, having experienced a period of art-world success, had her own breakdown after returning to Tokyo permanently in 1973
Two years later, she checked herself in to a psychiatric institution, where she became a permanent resident from 1977 until her death

The institution was within walking distance of her multistory studio. [ Read: An artist for the Instagram age ] Her psychic travails had to do with her upbringing (she had an authoritarian mother and an unfaithful father), which left her afraid of sex and intimacy
She suffered from severe audiovisual hallucinations, in which she would see flashing lights, auras, and dense fields of dots
She fell into deep episodes of clinical depression and attempted suicide twice

When Kusama reemerged as an active artist in 1989, she and her supporters presented her mental-health issues not just as an important aspect of her personal story but as part of the energy that fueled her artwork
All of this was healthy frankness, but it also undoubtedly enhanced her work’s reception
People could relate to the idea of creativity as a function of—and therapy for—mental illness

Kusama and her promoters emphasized the link, tapping into narratives about the artist as a suffering visionary that went back to Van Gogh and even earlier artists (including such figures as Piero di Cosimo, Caravaggio, and Rosso Fiorentino) whose artistic brilliance was linked to their strange behavior and (perhaps) mental instability
In the 20th century, the idea of a connection between creativity and interior turmoil was taken up with renewed gusto, and the category of outsider art (or art brut) was established
Outsider artists could reconnect us to the amputated life of the emotions, re-enchanting a world diagnosed by Max Weber, in 1917, as disenchanted
Kusama was one of many artists who swam with these currents
She talked about her repeating dots as an expression of an inclination toward “self-obliteration”—an urge to dissolve into forever-expanding patterns
The idea sounded at once mystical, therapeutic, and nightmarish

title: What Dolly Parton Knew About Reading
excerpt: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
body: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
My best friend’s baby got mail from Dolly Parton on the day the singer died
This wasn’t unexpected: He’s been receiving books from Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library for all 10 months of his life. (This month’s selection was Bedtime, Here I Come , by D
Steinberg.) And he wasn’t alone—the Imagination Library sends free books to children every month from birth to age 5; the program has passed out more than 300 million books in five countries
My colleague Annie Joy Williams wrote earlier this week about the legacy of Parton —and her books program—in Tennessee, the home state that all three of us share
But the Imagination Library has expanded far beyond that territory

When I lived in an apartment building in Washington, D.C., I would see books bearing the library’s distinctive seal on a table in the lobby—volumes too big for my neighbor’s mailbox, quietly awaiting little hands

First, here are three new stories from The Atlantic ’s Books section: Portrait of the artist as a movie star “Tallying,” a poem by Joanna Klink “Wilderness Years,” a poem by Dave Lucas The progress that can’t be erased Stories about Parton’s generosity are spreading widely: She helped fund a COVID-19 vaccine and filmed herself getting the shot when many Americans were hesitant
She opened a sanctuary for bald eagles! She did so many things for so many kinds of Americans, and especially Tennesseans, that I find it hard to keep track

But she said, many times, that she’d be happy to be remembered not as a generational talent or a dolled-up diva but as “the book lady.” Parton grew up in poverty in East Tennessee, and she frequently cited her illiterate father as the inspiration for her books program, which she founded in 1995

I don’t know whether all of Parton’s fans knew how high she ranked literacy on her list of important causes, but when I watched tributes to Parton roll in this week, I noted that people I’d grown up with in Tennessee (mostly young women like me) kept posting the same tableaus on Instagram: photos of babies and kids sitting with their parents, reading a book they’d gotten from the Imagination Library
The photos are cute—but they also reflect something deeply important

A few years ago, I edited an essay by the children’s-book author Katherine Marsh that identified one reason young kids were less motivated to read: Schools often push them toward a “hyperfocus on analysis” and give precedence to individual paragraphs and sentences rather than entire narratives
But, Marsh argues, “the best way to present an abstract idea to kids is by hooking them on a story.” And a great way to get a kid interested in a story is by reading it aloud to them

In another article, published a year ago, Ilana Kurshan wrote about this declining but important practice , and about doing it with her son: “The delight of reading to him lay not in the pages we turned,” she wrote, “but in the wheels that seemed to turn in his mind as we read together.” Thanks to my friends’ beloved babies and the perks of my job— which have included putting together a list of essential children’s books —I’ve been thinking a lot about the importance of reading with children
They still encounter books in schools and libraries, but Parton’s program emphasized building a bookshelf at home, where caregivers and kids can share stories as part of a daily routine
Reading aloud offers a child more than the chance to develop literacy skills

It gave Kurshan, for example, “a way to guide them as they started to understand the world, and as I started to understand them.” So, like Parton, I’ll be happy if kids see me as a “book lady.” Last week, I bought a picture book about berries for a different toddler
And although my friend’s 10-month-old already has plenty at home, I couldn’t resist mailing him a few more books
Peter Marlow / Magnum What Parents Lose When They Don’t Read to Their Kids By Ilana Kurshan Sharing books with my children was about a lot more than literacy

What to Read Hippos Go Berserk! , by Sandra Boynton Hippos Go Berserk! , a sterling example of Boynton’s comedic genius, has the subtitle “A wild counting story.” “One hippo, all alone, calls two hippos on the phone,” it begins, and each page introduces another attendee to a gathering being planned in real time, until 45 of them crowd an all-night cocktail party
Then come the visual gags: There’s a hippo’s version of Whistler’s Mother , a hippo upside-down, and one guest, a classic spiky-furred grinning Boynton beastie, who consistently eludes the count

As the hippos gradually leave, little creature in tow, Berserk shows that even basic arithmetic can be an act of imagination, rather than rote repetition—and it cleverly reminds adult readers that the most familiar exercise can invite unexpected images into the mind. — Walt Hunter From our list: 65 essential children’s books Out Next Week 📚 The Castle: Adventures in a World of Unraveling Men , by Jon Ronson 📚 I Liked Rex , by Diane Williams 📚 All the Hidden Places , by Cadwell Turnbull Your Weekend Read The painter Milton Avery Arnold

Newman Properties / Getty The Painter Who Shaped Rothko By Sebastian Smee Beginning in the early 1930s, three Americans—Milton Avery, Mark Rothko, and Adolph Gottlieb—began spending summers together on Cape Ann, along the coast of northeast Massachusetts
They loved the gritty authenticity of Gloucester, the nation’s oldest fishing port
Cape Ann’s distinctive, undulant geography combined pungent industry and village intensity with Atlantic immensity of sea and sky
The story of the relationships among these artists, in particular between the older Avery and the now–stratospherically famous Rothko, shows us American modernism in its moment of greatest transition

title: The AI Backlash Gets Professional
excerpt: I f there’s one thing America seems to agree on, it’s AI
body: I f there’s one thing America seems to agree on, it’s AI

Some three-quarters of Americans oppose a data center being built in their area, three-quarters of Americans think AI will hurt their job security, nearly 70 percent think the technology is advancing too quickly—the polls go on
Progressive and Republican candidates alike are bashing the tech industry to win primary elections
States and cities are halting plans for data-center development

Yet in cloistered San Francisco, where I live, staffers at OpenAI and Anthropic are developing this same feared technology at light speed and pulling down compensation packages that stretch to considerably more than $1 million
Silicon Valley’s growth is largely unencumbered by regulation, and President Trump’s administration has if anything used its authority to speed the AI industry along

The divide between these camps—the majority of people in this country who simply have to deal with the technology as it’s rolled out, and the much smaller population of people with direct influence over it—is a defining feature of this era

And so I noticed when a small group, with ties to both the Bay Area and Washington, started making noise, insisting that the AI race slow down and the technology be overseen not by executives and engineers, but by the broadest population possible
The group—which formally launched today and calls itself Irreplaceable, as in people are irreplaceable by machines —has an audacious and perhaps naive vision
It is essentially a protest against capitalism as it is practiced in America today, focused on resisting first and developing a coherent plan for the future later

I have seen exactly how bulletproof the AI companies are—pilfering seemingly infinite volumes of media to train their models, building unpermitted power plants for their data centers, and unleashing autonomous agents capable of massive security breaches, almost entirely without consequence

I wanted to meet with Irreplaceable’s founders to ask: How do they possibly expect to pull this off? [ Read: It may be time to panic about AI ] The organization is staffed with people who made a name for themselves in the climate movement, and they are hoping to avoid past mistakes by focusing on the emotional reaction Americans are having to AI, rather than anchoring their work in white papers and policy recommendations. “People get it,” Jeremy Ornstein—a campaign strategist for Irreplaceable and former organizer with the Sunrise Movement—told me. “People have the intuition that if we create machines more powerful than people, that could go dangerously and terribly wrong.” Phil Aroneanu, Irreplaceable’s executive director and a co-founder of the climate organization 350.org , told me he believes that climate advocates initially floundered because they acted as policy wonks
They thought that making evidence-based arguments about the dangers of melting ice sheets and rising sea levels to receptive congresspeople would be enough to pass nationwide climate legislation
Today, Aroneanu said, movements are built not necessarily on what people think, but instead on what they feel
For climate, that meant fossil-fuel-divestment campaigns, protesting oil pipelines, and the school strikes led by Greta Thunberg

People are already “feeling the squeeze,” Aroneanu told me. “And we should be pointing that anxiety and that anger in the right direction.” Irreplaceable will prioritize a range of issues: mitigating automation’s effects on the economy, protecting against government and corporate use of AI to surveil Americans, and establishing industry oversight and guardrails to prevent catastrophic disasters, such as widespread blackouts caused by AI-powered hacking or bot-engineered pandemics

As I spoke with the activists, I kept thinking about what had become of the climate movement—the Green New Deal passed, but only after being watered down, and it was then gutted by the second Trump administration—but their populist approach makes sense

Some of the biggest and perhaps only lasting successes over the past 15 years of American politics—the Tea Party, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, MAGA, and election denialism—have been fueled by outrage over an unfair economy and seemingly rigged politics
These organizers have demonstrated their ability to win significant battles
Sunrise, 350.org, and others were instrumental in passing national legislation, galvanizing widespread climate demonstrations, and accelerating private-sector development of renewable energy
And Irreplacable’s members have already flexed some muscle when it comes to AI
In July, hundreds of people gathered for what was likely the largest anti-AI demonstration in San Francisco’s history, marching from OpenAI’s headquarters to Anthropic’s and finally to Google’s
A few months earlier, some of these “Stop the AI Race” organizers had staged a somewhat disorganized protest: Attendees at times struggled to chant in unison
The second time around, the march was advised by Ornstein, and attendees had chant sheets, a marching band, and a slushy truck (to “freeze” AI)

Already, a number of climate-oriented groups (including the environmental-justice arm of the NAACP as well as the Sierra Club and Earthjustice) are supporting local data-center battles by filing lawsuits, shaping model legislation, and organizing protests

The overlap is both concrete—data centers pollute the air and burn fossil fuels for their tremendous electricity demands—and thematic: a movement against corporate interests to change or regulate the technology of the future

At least on a local level, the groups are finding victories: Dozens of data centers have been canceled in the face of local opposition, and all of the major AI companies have promised to pay extra to avoid hiking up local electricity bills
In Michigan, both Abdul El-Sayed and William Lawrence, who is a co-founder of Sunrise, won Democratic primaries as progressive candidates hammering against data centers
Still, this bubbling AI anxiety is far from a sweeping tide
That growing numbers of Americans are concerned about AI development does not mean they are concerned for similar or even compatible reasons
People may say they loathe data centers, but they might also enjoy the conveniences of AI products at home or work
They fear bots getting too powerful, too quickly, but also think America needs to stay ahead of China in AI development
At one anti-AI protest, I saw people who were ostensibly on the same side disagree about AI’s water use and whether certain jobs would be better off automated by chatbots
And to the extent that a sufficiently powerful AI movement would need to be global, just as climate organizing was, the technology generally polls much better outside the U.S

The AI backlash is to some extent an American phenomenon, which bodes poorly for any sort of global norms or treaties. [ From the April 2026 issue: Inside the dirty, dystopian world of AI data centers ] When pressed, nobody from Irreplaceable and no other climate activists turning to AI would articulate a concrete AI agenda. “We’ve aligned around saying no,” Lawrence recently told me. “Now, there is an important conversation that is yet to come, about— okay, so what do we want? ” This is, for now, a significant weakness; a key turning point for the climate movement was providing a positive vision, the Green New Deal, for both decarbonizing and reinvigorating the American economy
Being able to link every data-center battle and primary campaign to a national vision would give the AI backlash some form
It’s not wrong to want to develop a policy road map with the input of a broad coalition; climate advocates took decades to devise and unite around the Green New Deal
Irreplaceable’s stated plan is to build a coalition this year, develop a unified policy next year, and implement that agenda by the end of 2029
Measured against any metric other than Silicon Valley’s warp speed, that would be fast

But those few years will leave plenty of time for tech companies to push back—they’ve already spent tens of millions of dollars leading up to the midterms—and regardless, by then OpenAI, Anthropic, and any number of Chinese firms may already have built and lost control of even more powerful models

title: The Crisis for Democrats in Michigan
excerpt: ET on August 28, 2026 T he hard-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker warned Jewish Americans last week that their excessive identification with Israel would subject
body: ET on August 28, 2026 T he hard-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker warned Jewish Americans last week that their excessive identification with Israel would subject them to anti-Semitic attacks. “If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action—not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews,” he said

Piker’s tone was one of rueful concern, not unlike the pose adopted by anti-Semites throughout history. “No person with a sense of the dignity of mankind can condone the persecution of the Jewish race in Germany

But no person of honesty and vision can look on their pro-war policy here today without seeing the dangers involved in such a policy both for us and for them,” the Nazi sympathizer Charles Lindbergh said in 1941

Several leading Democrats, including Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, issued statements denouncing Piker’s ugly warning to the Jews as a barely veiled anti-Semitic threat
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat running for Michigan’s other Senate seat, trod more carefully

He issued a statement “in response to Hasan Piker’s comments” affirming that “all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence” and denouncing anti-Semitism, but the statement itself did not say whether Piker’s comment qualified as anti-Semitism

El-Sayed instead dismissed Piker as a distraction, saying at a recent rally, “The effort to make this race about a streamer in L.A. is actually kind of laughable.” Most Democrats followed El-Sayed’s line that Piker was irrelevant. “This election is about what’s going to happen when we elect Abdul to the United States Senate
I am done, so don’t any reporter ask me again about Hasan Piker
It’s not what November is about,” Representative Debbie Dingell said at a rally for El-Sayed. [ Graeme Wood: Something is happening to America’s moral code ] Democrats have good reason to say this
El-Sayed is running a close race to hold a seat that Democrats probably need to retain to win control of the Senate in the midterm elections
But the truth is that Piker, and the uncomfortable questions raised by his alliance with El-Sayed, is one of the important questions at stake in the election
If Piker were just an internet pundit, his rant—the latest entry in a long list of outrageous comments he has made—would be of little consequence to the Democratic Party

Piker has said that “America deserved 9/11,” praised Mao Zedong as “one of the great leaders of this world,” and mourned the collapse of the Soviet Union as “one of the greatest catastrophes of the 20th century.” His ideology is profoundly authoritarian
But several left-wing Democrats, especially El-Sayed, have campaigned with Piker and elevated him into one of their most prominent surrogates
So El-Sayed’s alliance with Piker has become a political and moral crisis
In Michigan, Democrats are trying to avoid handing Republicans their first Senate win in the state in more than three decades
But if El-Sayed wins, he would throw open the doors of the party to a strain of militant politics that many Jews justifiably consider dangerous
The Democratic Party is now divided between those who are trying to force El-Sayed to stop encouraging left-wing anti-Semites and those who give him their unconditional support
T he Michigan Senate election has presented liberals with a grim choice
The Republican candidate, Mike Rogers, has pledged support for a corrupt, racist, authoritarian-minded administration
Rogers hasn’t made even the tiniest concession to Donald Trump critics
But supporting El-Sayed means accepting a strain of anti-Semitic politics that to date has had no place within the Democratic Party
What’s more, El-Sayed has already said that he intends to use his victory as a platform to reshape the party
Him winning could invite a future in which the United States has not just one party that is open to bigots but two

Although El-Sayed has never said anything nearly as inflammatory as the sorts of comments Piker makes routinely, his mixture of anti-Zionism and populism treats pro-Israel activism as a nefarious and all-pervasive force
He has denied that any Democrat who believes in human rights could have any motive other than money for holding a position on Israel different from the one he prefers
El-Sayed tends to depict nearly all opposition to his candidacy as financially driven, but when applied to Jewish political activity, this charge becomes even more conspiratorial
Ann Arbor, where El-Sayed lives, is home to a branch of the Free Palestine movement that has engaged in violent intimidation of Jewish Democrats

Activists at the University of Michigan not only seized the central campus grounds for their own but also vandalized the business of Jordan Acker, a Democratic regent, and made middle-of-the-night attacks on his home, one of which involved shattering his window with a jar of urine
El-Sayed has campaigned on the Michigan campus with Amir Makled, a lawyer who defended the protesters and who has shared anti-Semitic and pro-Hezbollah social-media posts

When the Justice Department charged eight of the protesters—one of whom had worked on El-Sayed’s campaign—in a plot to commit still more acts of intimidation, El-Sayed treated the indictment as biased, telling reporters, “It’s a lot more about what you’re advocating for that gets you indicted or not indicted, rather than what you did.” Dana Nessel, the state’s attorney general, has faced anti-Semitic harassment and has said that she plans to skip the state party’s August convention rather than endure more abuse
At the party’s April nominating caucus, Mallory McMorrow, a then-candidate for Senate, reported that her Jewish husband was subjected to an anti-Semitic slur

On the weekend before the primary, Walter Masterson, a left-wing streamer who has appeared with El-Sayed, disrupted an event for Haley Stevens, El-Sayed’s pro-Israel opponent in the Democratic primary, forcing the brewery hosting it to cancel the event
El-Sayed did not condemn the bully-boy tactics used on his behalf

Before he warned American Jews that they were bringing anti-Semitism on themselves by identifying with Israel, Piker displayed on his Twitch stream a quote attributed to Jeremy Moss, the Democratic nominee for Congress in a suburban Detroit district: “The entire purpose of my campaign is to make sure America continues to support Israel
I don’t think it’s wrong for Jews in America to want to put Israel first
America is not our homeland and we have been victims of antisemitism here.” Moss insists that the quote is a pure fabrication, and no one has yet produced any evidence of its authenticity
Numerous Democrats denounced Piker’s comments

Instead of apologizing, though, Piker replied on X , “Aipac boss call was made,” implying that only the influence of the pro-Israel lobby could have caused Democrats to object to his rhetoric. [ James Loeffler: The hatred that broke American politics ] El-Sayed has refused pleas from his fellow Democrats to break off his alliance with Piker, who joined him at a pool party on the last day of campaigning before the primary

El-Sayed first brushed off the requests by likening Piker to Joe Rogan, a controversial podcaster whose show some Democrats have appeared on (but not a figure they have brought out on the campaign trail)

title: The Download: a secretive antiaging drug and joining virtual power plants
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

A startup claims it’s found a drug to make your blood young —Antonio Regalado I knew I’d officially become a “longevity influencer” when a company called Generation Lab offered me the chance to write about—and even receive—their new rejuvenation treatment
This wasn’t just any antiaging treatment, either

A company fact sheet says that it “blocks the systemic spread of aging in the bloodstream, reawakens the body’s own repair mechanism and restores health and youth to multiple tissues.” The approach is based on research by Generation Lab’s irascible scientific founder, Irina Conboy
She found that joining the circulatory systems of old and young mice improved the old animals’ ability to heal from injury
Conboy now says she has found a combination of two existing drugs that can produce youthful effects without the need for any bodily fluid exchange
But Generation Lab won’t reveal what the drugs are, making the proposition hard to take seriously
Read the full story on the drug combo that claims to “stop the spread of aging.” How to sign up for a virtual power plant—and decide whether you should Your thermostat may not look like a power plant
Neither does your electric vehicle, home battery, or HVAC system
But utility and energy companies increasingly want to treat them like one

That’s the idea behind a virtual power plant , or VPP, a collection of household devices (such as smart thermostats, EV chargers, and solar panels) that a utility can control, usually by commanding them to draw less electricity during peak hours
In exchange, participants receive a discount on their energy bills and, in some cases, a signing bonus
Here’s how to sign up for a VPP—and decide whether it’s worth it . —Eshan Raul This story is part of MIT Technology Review’s How To series, which gives you practical advice on getting things done

The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 A judge has blocked the Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic The court found the designation violated First Amendment rights. ( NYT $) + And ruled that the designation was based on retaliation. ( CNBC ) + Anthropic still faces a separate case in Washington, DC. ( Reuters $) + The Pentagon’s culture war against Anthropic backfired. ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Tech giants have called for a defensive surge to defeat AI-driven hacks Over 100 companies warned that a wave of cyberattacks is imminent. ( BBC ) + And urged government and industry leaders to take rapid action. ( Quartz ) + Their main solution, unsurprisingly, is more AI. ( Gizmodo ) + Here’s why OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 Anthropic has launched an AI tool that conducts scientific experiments It lets AI agents autonomously operate microscopes, lasers, and robotic arms. ( FT $) + And includes rules designed for safe operations in labs. ( Wired $) + It’s Anthropic’s first tool designed for the physical world. ( Ars Technica ) 4 India’s data center boom is leaving the people it displaces with nothing Policymakers courting Big Tech are sidelining local communities. ( Rest of World ) + No one wants a data center in their backyard. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 OpenAI is testing a “persistent” AI agent that keeps working Codex could continue tasks until it’s “put to sleep.” ( Wired $) + And generate follow-up tasks without prompting. ( Gizmodo ) 6 A lawsuit alleges that Grok was trained on child sexual abuse material It claims victims’ images entered the chatbot’s training data. ( Ars Technica ) + A federal judge says AI has outpaced child-abuse laws. ( WP $) 7 AI writing has reached a turning point in the media Sparked by the Wall Street Journal defending an AI-written op-ed. ( Atlantic $) 8 China’s robotic racers are exposing the limits of human speed Their advances are revealing what our bodies can’t do. ( Reuters $) 9 Young workers are turning to “AI-proof” traditional crafts They’re drawn to creative, hands-on skills that tech can’t easily replicate. ( Guardian ) 10 Scientists have a new army to fight invasive crabs: 150,000 baby octopuses Italian researchers just released the animals into the Adriatic Sea. ( New Scientist $) Quote of the day “ The academic record is being quietly haunted.”  —A new preprint research paper from Samsung and the University of Warsaw warns that a torrent of AI-generated study papers written by fake researchers is contaminating academic publishing

One more thing The problem with thinking you’re part Neanderthal There’s a theory that many of us have an “inner Neanderthal.” The idea is that Homo sapiens and a cousin species once bred, leaving some people today with a trace of Neanderthal DNA.  This DNA is arguably the 21st century’s most celebrated discovery in human evolution

But in 2024, a pair of French geneticists called into question the theory’s very foundations.  They proposed that what scientists interpret as interbreeding could instead be explained by population structure—the way genes concentrate in smaller, isolated groups

Find out what it all means for human evolution . —Ben Crair We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + Check out the dazzling photos in this year’s Wildlife Photographer of the Year . + Bowerbirds in Australia are turning human trash into treasure to impress females. + A Los Angeles Costco parking lot has become a low-risk skate park for the over-40s . + The Listening Museum has lovingly curated and sound-mapped acoustic signatures of mechanical keyboards.

title: How to sign up for a virtual power plant—and decide whether you should
excerpt: MIT Technology Review ’s How To series helps you get things done.  Your thermostat may not look like a power plant
body: MIT Technology Review ’s How To series helps you get things done.  Your thermostat may not look like a power plant
Neither does your electric vehicle, home battery, or HVAC system
But utility and energy companies increasingly want to treat them like one
A virtual power plant , or VPP, is a collection of household devices (such as smart thermostats, electric-vehicle chargers, home batteries, and solar panels) that a utility can control
Usually that means commanding the devices to draw less electricity during peak hours

For example, the utility might adjust your thermostat or delay or slow EV charging when electricity demand is high.  In exchange, the utility offers VPP participants a discount on their energy bills and, in some cases, a signing bonus

Seth Frader-Thompson, CEO and cofounder of EnergyHub, a software company that helps utility companies run VPP programs, says a smart thermostat program may offer an initial bonus of roughly $50 to $150, plus about $25 to $50 per year, while home battery and EV devices could yield hundreds or thousands of dollars in annual savings
The amount of power the utility might throttle in any one home is small

But it adds up, Frader-Thompson says. “When you put it together at the scale of hundreds of thousands, or millions, it has a pretty profound impact,” he says, equivalent to “firing up a power plant.” As of 2023 , there were already more than 500 VPP programs operating in the US alone, and the number has only grown since, especially with big players like Google starting to invest in this technology to help power their data centers

An estimated 4 million households with smart thermostats were enrolled in a VPP program as of last year.  But the approach is still new, and some programs may still have some kinks to work out, says Severin Borenstein, faculty director of UC Berkeley’s Energy Institute at Haas and member of the board of governors of the California Independent System Operator, which manages most of the state’s electric grid

If a program is not implemented well, he says, a utility may incorrectly predict when VPP participants plan to use more electricity and pay them for not using energy they weren’t planning to use anyway, potentially increasing energy bills for nonparticipants
Still, Borenstein says, “if we do it well, I think it can really be a benefit,” one that could help utilities avoid an expensive grid upgrade or emergency measures to conserve power
Most consumer VPPs today are less dramatic than the name suggests and don’t actively send energy from your EV or home battery to the grid
But battery-to-grid programs are on the rise—and potentially offer even larger savings for consumers in the future
So how do you actually sign up for a VPP? And how do you know if it’s worth it? 1
Check whether your utility company has a program and, if so, whether it actually supports your devices
The types and brands of home devices supported vary from program to program
Your utility’s website is the obvious place to look to see if yours qualifies, but it’s important to note that you may not actually see the phrase “virtual power plant” anywhere

You may have better luck searching for your utility’s name plus terms like “demand response,” “peak rewards,” “connected solutions,” “battery storage,” “smart thermostat rewards,” “managed charging,” or “bring your own device.” But don’t stop with the utility, Frader-Thompson says: “The way most people actually learn about this and sign up is through the manufacturer of the device they have.” In other words, the offer may show up through your smart thermostat app, EV app, or battery app, or in an email from the company that made the device

Once you find a program, the instructions for enrollment may be as simple as clicking through an app, filling out a utility form, or confirming your account and device information through a third-party enrollment page
EV drivers may be able to see the terms and payment in their automaker app and enroll “with a click of a button,” says Joseph Vellone, CEO of the EV-focused VPP company ChargeScape

A smart thermostat program could require an approved Wi-Fi thermostat; an EV program may depend on your automaker, charger, utility territory, or rate plan; a battery program may depend on the battery brand, inverter, or installer and whether your system can communicate with the utility
These programs are also not evenly distributed across the country

Most programs are established in places with lots of flexible devices, stressed grids, supportive utilities, or strong state policies—especially California, Texas, New England, and increasingly parts of the mid-Atlantic region. 2.  Ask yourself how much flexibility you can afford
Before you sign up for a VPP, you’ll want to determine whether you’re willing to let a company adjust a device in your home—even if it typically happens only a few times a week
For some people, this may be an easy decision: If your EV sits plugged in all night but only needs two hours to charge, shifting when that charging happens may be almost invisible
A home battery program could be lucrative if you understand how often the battery will be used, how much backup power you can keep, and whether extra cycling affects your equipment

Other households, however, “do not have the flexibility to engage in one of these programs,” says Sanya Carley, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania and faculty director of the Climate Center for Energy Policy

She says that people who work night shifts, have caregiving responsibilities or health needs, or are already aggressively limiting their energy use to save money may have less room to allow a utility to adjust heating, cooling, or charging rates during peak hours for grid demand.  3
Review the opt-out rules and read the fine print
VPP programs generally give participants the ability to override temporary changes made by the utility
This right to “opt out” is what makes them workable for many customers

Can you skip a day of the program on your thermostat if you’re planning to have guests over? Can you tell your car to charge immediately before a long road trip? Can you keep a battery reserve for outages? Utilities are typically motivated to make the opt-out process as simple as possible, with few rules and restrictions
It could also be worth investigating where your data might be going

EV and battery programs may need to collect data about things like charging status and schedule, or how much power a device is drawing, while smart thermostat data may reveal patterns about when people are home, sleeping, or using appliances.The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit focused on digital rights, has warned that this data could be used to infer private routines inside a home; depending on the program, that information may not only move through a utility but get distributed to device manufacturers, software platforms, or third parties involved in running the program
ChargeScape and Energy Hub say the data used for these programs is limited and functional
EV data is focused on “the physics and the energy of the asset itself,” Vellone says
Frader-Thompson explains,“It doesn’t really matter what any one customer is doing
It matters what the average customer is doing.” 4
Decide whether the offer is worth it for you

title: Dolly Parton took control of her career by making men the butt of the joke
url:
<title>Dolly Parton took control of her career by making men the butt of the joke</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756635/original/file-20260827-60-ghsows.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=469%2C274%2C2367%2C1578&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Dolly Parton was fond of saying, &#39;It takes a lot of money to look this cheap.&#39;</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/dolly-parton-at-the-phil-donahue-show-at-wgn-television-in-news-photo/950456848?adppopup=true">Paul Natkin/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Of all the moments that capture Dolly Parton’s musical talents, fierce intelligence and driving ambition, I often find myself thinking back to an awkward, ad-libbed live television duet on “<a href="https://tennesseeencyclopedia.net/entries/the-porter-wagoner-show/">The Porter Wagoner Show</a>.”</p>

<p>The year was 1973. Parton had been performing <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2007/10/30/arts/music/30wagoner.html">alongside Wagoner</a> on the syndicated variety show since 1967. Though this had been her big break in Nashville, Parton was feeling confined by playing second fiddle to Wagoner, who, as her producer, often <a href="https://www.press.uillinois.edu/books/?id=p085420">took control of the musical arrangements of her songs</a>. Despite Parton’s commercial success, he was often dismissive of her creative vision. </p>

<p>With Parton and Wagoner set to perform “<a href="https://genius.com/Dolly-parton-run-that-by-me-one-more-time-lyrics">Run That By Me One More Time</a>” – a song Parton had written in 1970, about a marital quarrel – Wagoner begins by saying, “Me and my sidekick, she just kicked me in the side.” Dolly retorts, “Not yet, but I think I will after this.”</p>

<p>After the two sing the opening lines, Parton dives into her verse:  </p>

<blockquote>
<p>“Well you’re late again I see</p>

<p>What’s your excuse this time?</p>

<p>Don’t try to kiss and make up</p>

<p>When you smell so strong from wine.”</p>
</blockquote>

<p>Right as Wagoner moves in to sing his excuse for coming home late, Parton unexpectedly interrupts him by singing a prolonged, “Well, I –” as if she were going to sing another line. Porter, caught by surprise, pauses. Parton laughs, “I thought I’d throw that in.” A flustered Wagoner asks Parton where they are in the song. </p>

<p>Back on track, Wagoner begins the next verse, demanding to know what Parton has done with the rent money. She ad-libs her explanation: “You seen me put that money in that cookie jar the same day you brought it home and one day I come back from shopping and I looked and every dime of that money was gone but I didn’t get it and you know I didn’t get it.”</p>

<p>She’s gone well over her allotted time, and Wagoner starts singing his planned retort. But Parton doesn’t let up and starts speaking over him: “I didn’t get it. I don’t know who got it but I don’t want you packing it on me no more.”  </p>

<p>Guffaws are audible from the crowd. All Wagoner can do is awkwardly laugh as he says, “Would you run – me by that one more time.” </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/BpeCa8rud3Q?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Dolly Parton and Porter Wagoner perform ‘Run That By Me One More Time’ on a 1973 episode of ‘The Porter Wagoner Show.’</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Wagoner eventually recovers and the two cheerfully finish the song to applause. But for anyone watching, it’s clear who’s in control and whose song it is.</p>

<p>A year later, Parton left the show after writing the hit songs “<a href="https://genius.com/Dolly-parton-jolene-lyrics">Jolene</a>” and “<a href="https://genius.com/Dolly-parton-i-will-always-love-you-lyrics">I Will Always Love You</a>.” Her 1976 album, “All I Can Do,” was nominated for a Grammy for Best Country Vocal Performance, Female. </p>

<p>The rest – <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/entertainment/music/articles/dolly-parton-25-no-1-191704206.html">25 No. 1 country singles</a>, <a href="https://www.grammy.com/artists/dolly-parton/17205/">10 Grammy awards</a>, <a href="https://www.bmi.com/news/bmi-remembers-country-music-legend-bmi-icon-dolly-parton">44 Top 10 country albums</a> – is history.</p>

<h2>Turning the tables</h2>

<p>Parton, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/25/arts/music/dolly-parton-dead.html">who died on Aug. 25, 2026</a>, didn’t simply tell jokes for cheap chuckles.</p>

<p><a href="https://arts-sciences.buffalo.edu/global-gender-sexuality/faculty/faculty-directory.host.html/content/shared/arts-sciences/global-gender-sexuality/faculty-profiles/vander-wel-stephanie.html">In my work as a scholar of country music</a>, I’ve written about how female country artists from the mid-20th century to the 2010s deployed humor to elbow their way into an industry that has often been hostile to women.</p>

<p>Throughout the genre’s history, female country artists <a href="https://books.google.com/books/about/Finding_Her_Voice.html?id=7QcJAQAAMAAJ">could be treated as window dressing</a> for the male main attractions. And when women did achieve success, the industry could be quick to portray them as climbers who abandoned their country roots in pursuit of pop stardom.</p>

<p>Women also traditionally have had a harder time getting recording contracts and radio airplay. As recently as 2015, radio consultant Keith Hill controversially said that country stations <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/music/2015/may/27/saladgate-tomatoes-women-country-music">should play mostly male artists</a>, describing men as the “lettuce” and women as the “tomatoes” in a salad.</p>

<p>One way female artists fought back? By using humor to upend expectations about how women should behave.</p>

<p>In Lulu Belle’s comedic take on marriage in her 1939 song “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zm4dllYJBmc">I Wish I Was a Single Girl Again</a>,” she plays the part of the female rube. By assuming the caricature of female hillbilly, she was able to do or say things that a conventionally respectable female character couldn’t.</p>

<p>Similarly, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/news/2003/may/17/guardianobituaries.artsobituaries">June Carter</a> often played the unruly country girl who aimed her punchlines at male hosts and duet partners, including Johnny Cash. And in the uproarious “<a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/whose-country-music/pistol-annies/96CF8D4976D4976302876C75A731996E">Got My Name Changed Back</a>,” the contemporary trio Pistol Annies use humor to turn the pain of divorce into a celebration of female empowerment. </p>

<p>But few have ever wielded humor as deftly as Parton. She used quick-witted retorts and self-deprecating jokes as weapons to disarm audiences and shine a spotlight on double standards and gendered biases.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">

<p>She often did this by making men the butt of her jokes.</p>

<p>Take two of Parton’s first commercial hits: “Dumb Blonde,” written by Curly Putman, and her self-penned “Something Fishy.”</p>

<p>In “<a href="https://genius.com/Dolly-parton-dumb-blonde-lyrics">Dumb Blonde</a>,” Parton tells the story of a cheating man who, upon being confronted, angrily accuses her of being a “dumb blonde.” After announcing that “this dumb blonde ain’t nobody’s fool,” the song’s narrator triumphantly declares, “If there’s one thing this blonde has learned, blondes have more fun,” before walking away from the relationship on her own terms.</p>

<p>“<a href="https://genius.com/Dolly-parton-something-fishy-lyrics">Something Fishy</a>” is another song about a cheater. Parton’s lyrics contrast the man’s thin lies about “going on fishing trips” with her suspicion of his infidelities. </p>

<p>“Something fishy is going on,” she says wryly, playing up the pun. The audience is in on the mockery of this dim-witted man, whose astute wife can see right through him. </p>

<h2>Dolly’s world</h2>

<p>In the same way that Parton took the spotlight from Wagoner during that televised duet in 1973 – and makes it clear who’s in control and who isn’t – Parton also took control of the narrative of her career. When critics <a href="https://theconversation.com/dolly-parton-changed-country-music-by-refusing-to-play-by-its-rules-290691">questioned her commitment to country</a>, she demonstrated that popular stardom and country authenticity were not mutually exclusive. When they condemned her ambition, she made no apologies for wanting more. <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/aug/26/dolly-parton-style-fashion">When they tried to ridicule her look</a>, she owned her Dolly image by means of her wit.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/aug/25/dolly-parton-best-quotes">As Parton would often say</a>, “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap.”</p>

<p>There’s so much in that line. For one, it’s hilarious. But it also signals that she intentionally crafted her campy persona, and that her calculated appearance also contributed to her wild success.</p>

<p>That was Dolly: self-deprecating, self-aware, self-assured and, yes – wickedly funny.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290574/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Paul Natkin/Getty Images Of all the moments that capture Dolly Parton’s musical talents, fierce intelligence and driving ambition, I often find myself thinking back to an awkward, ad-libbed live television duet on “ The Porter Wagoner Show .” The year was 1973
Parton had been performing alongside Wagoner on the syndicated variety show since 1967
Though this had been her big break in Nashville, Parton was feeling confined by playing second fiddle to Wagoner, who, as her producer, often took control of the musical arrangements of her songs
Despite Parton’s commercial success, he was often dismissive of her creative vision

With Parton and Wagoner set to perform “ Run That By Me One More Time ” – a song Parton had written in 1970, about a marital quarrel – Wagoner begins by saying, “Me and my sidekick, she just kicked me in the side.” Dolly retorts, “Not yet, but I think I will after this.” After the two sing the opening lines, Parton dives into her verse: “Well you’re late again I see What’s your excuse this time? Don’t try to kiss and make up When you smell so strong from wine.” Right as Wagoner moves in to sing his excuse for coming home late, Parton unexpectedly interrupts him by singing a prolonged, “Well, I –” as if she were going to sing another line
Parton laughs, “I thought I’d throw that in.” A flustered Wagoner asks Parton where they are in the song
Back on track, Wagoner begins the next verse, demanding to know what Parton has done with the rent money

She ad-libs her explanation: “You seen me put that money in that cookie jar the same day you brought it home and one day I come back from shopping and I looked and every dime of that money was gone but I didn’t get it and you know I didn’t get it.” She’s gone well over her allotted time, and Wagoner starts singing his planned retort
But Parton doesn’t let up and starts speaking over him: “I didn’t get it
I don’t know who got it but I don’t want you packing it on me no more.” Guffaws are audible from the crowd

But for anyone watching, it’s clear who’s in control and whose song it is

A year later, Parton left the show after writing the hit songs “ Jolene ” and “ I Will Always Love You .” Her 1976 album, “All I Can Do,” was nominated for a Grammy for Best Country Vocal Performance, Female

Women also traditionally have had a harder time getting recording contracts and radio airplay

In Lulu Belle’s comedic take on marriage in her 1939 song “ I Wish I Was a Single Girl Again ,” she plays the part of the female rube
By assuming the caricature of female hillbilly, she was able to do or say things that a conventionally respectable female character couldn’t

<title>Lake Ontario to Lake America – who gets to decide what goes on maps?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756621/original/file-20260827-50-1dqcsa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C2%2C7201%2C4801&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">President Trump signed an executive order on Aug. 27, 2026, to rename Lake Ontario &#39;Lake America&#39; amid an ongoing trade war between the U.S. and Canada.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/map-labeling-lake-ontario-as-lake-america-is-displayed-as-u-news-photo/2292329268">Andrew Harnik/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>On Aug. 27, 2026, President Donald Trump issued an executive order <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/08/honoring-the-american-history-of-the-great-lakes-and-renaming-lake-ontario-as-lake-america/">renaming Lake Ontario</a> “Lake America,” <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6055425-lake-america-executive-order/">claiming his administration</a> had already “notified all of the various people you have to notify.”</p>

<p>The name change, which Ontario Premier Doug Ford had <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6055425-lake-america-executive-order/">dismissed as rhetoric</a> when it was first suggested, comes amid an <a href="https://theconversation.com/us-canada-trade-war-deepens-as-trump-revives-depression-era-trade-tool-whats-at-stake-for-consumers-and-the-midterms-290569">escalating trade war with Canada</a>. </p>

<p>Of course, this isn’t the first time Trump has renamed a location. In 2025 he issued an executive order to <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/restoring-names-that-honor-american-greatness/">rename the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America and return Alaska’s Denali</a>, the <a href="https://www.nationalgeographic.com/travel/national-parks/article/denali-national-park">tallest peak in the country</a>, to being called Mount McKinley. </p>

<p>While for some such renaming might seem less important than the big problems the country faces, there is a formal process in the United States for renaming places, and that process is taken seriously.</p>

<p>Usually, so people don’t get confused, the government uses official, agreed-upon names. In the U.S., place names are standardized by the <a href="https://www.usgs.gov/us-board-on-geographic-names">U.S. Board on Geographic Names</a>, which is part of the U.S. Geological Survey, the agency in charge of making maps. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/restoring-names-that-honor-american-greatness/">In his previous executive order</a>, Trump asked the Board on Geographic Names “to honor the contributions of visionary and patriotic Americans” and change its policies and procedures to reflect that. </p>

<p>Usually, renaming a place starts locally. The people in the state or county propose a name change and gather support. The process in each state is different. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/644766/original/file-20250124-17-6azvss.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A lake with sailboats and a city skyline in the background" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/644766/original/file-20250124-17-6azvss.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/644766/original/file-20250124-17-6azvss.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/644766/original/file-20250124-17-6azvss.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/644766/original/file-20250124-17-6azvss.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/644766/original/file-20250124-17-6azvss.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/644766/original/file-20250124-17-6azvss.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/644766/original/file-20250124-17-6azvss.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/minneapolis-minnesota-city-downtown-urban-skyline-royalty-free-image/172247249?phrase=Lake%20Calhoun&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">YinYang/E+ via Getty</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>How to change a place name</h2>

<p>In 2018, Minnesota <a href="https://www.minneapolisparks.org/news/2018/01/29/lake_calhoun_officially_recognized_as_bde_maka_ska/">changed the name of a large lake</a> in Minneapolis to Bde Maka Ska, which the Minneapolis Park Board described as “a Dakota name for the lake that has been passed down in oral history for many years.” </p>

<p>The board voted to change the name and took its request to the county commissioners. When the county agreed, the request was then sent to the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources, which <a href="https://www.startribune.com/the-state-officially-changes-lake-calhoun-to-bde-maka-ska/469990923">made it official for Minnesota</a>. Then, the state of Minnesota sent the request to the Board on Geographic Names, which made it <a href="http://www.startribune.com/feds-now-recognize-lake-calhoun-as-bde-maka-ska/488290241/">official for the entire U.S</a>.</p>

<p>It’s a lot of paperwork for something so seemingly minor, but people get passionate about place names. <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/01/22/climate/denali-mckinley-alaska-trump.html">It took 40 years</a> to rename Denali from the <a href="https://www.nps.gov/dena/learn/historyculture/denali-origins.htm">name established in the late 19th century</a>, Mount McKinley. </p>

<p>The state of Alaska <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2015/sep/01/alaska-natives-denali-name-change-decades">requested the name change in 1975</a>, but the Board on Geographic Names didn’t take action. Members of the Ohio congressional delegation – President William McKinley was from Ohio – <a href="https://alaskabeacon.com/2024/12/25/trumps-plan-to-revert-denali-to-mount-mckinley-name-irks-alaskans/">objected over many years</a> to requests to rename the mountain, and the board did not act on those requests. </p>

<p>The president appoints the <a href="https://theconversation.com/interior-secretary-manages-vast-lands-that-all-americans-share-and-can-sway-the-balance-between-conservation-and-development-245887">secretary of the Interior Department</a>. The secretary works with the heads of related agencies to appoint the Board on Geographic Names. Committee policy states, “<a href="https://d9-wret.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/assets/palladium/production/s3fs-public/media/files/DNC_PPP.pdf">Input from State geographic names authorities</a>, land management agencies, local governments, and Tribal Governments are actively pursued.”</p>

<p>In 2015, President Barack Obama named a new leader for the <a href="https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/blog/2013/02/06/president-obama-names-sally-jewell-lead-department-interior">Department of the Interior, Sally Jewell</a>. Just as Obama made a trip to <a href="https://www.adn.com/president-obama-in-alaska/article/obama-visits-snow-city-cafe-handshakes-pictures-and-1825-baked-goods-go/2015/09/02/">Alaska in late August 2015</a>, Jewell declared the name change official under a law that allows the secretary of the Interior to change a name if the <a href="https://www.usgs.gov/news/featured-story/old-name-officially-returns-nations-highest-peak">board doesn’t act on the proposal in a “reasonable” amount of time</a>.</p>



<p>“This name change <a href="https://www.usgs.gov/news/featured-story/old-name-officially-returns-nations-highest-peak">recognizes the sacred status of Denali</a> to many Alaska Natives,” Jewell said. “The name Denali has been official for use by the State of Alaska since 1975, but even more importantly, the mountain has been known as Denali for generations. With our own sense of reverence for this place, we are officially renaming the mountain Denali in recognition of the traditions of Alaska Natives and the strong support of the people of Alaska.”</p>



<p>If someone objects to a name change, they could ask the courts to rule on whether the name change was made legally. Going back to Bde Maka Ska, some people objected to changing the name from Lake Calhoun, <a href="https://www.greatlakesnow.org/2020/05/ap-supreme-court-dnr-name-lake-calhoun/">so they took the state natural resources agency to court</a>. Eventually, the Minnesota Supreme Court <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/minnesota/supreme-court/2020/a18-1007.html">ruled that the name change was done correctly</a>. </p>

<h2>How not to change a place name</h2>

<p>Renaming the Gulf of Mexico is a different kind of case, however, from renaming a geographic place within U.S. borders.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.nps.gov/guis/learn/nature/gulf-of-mexico.htm">The gulf is not within the territorial</a> United States. On the coast, <a href="https://www.noaa.gov/maritime-zones-and-boundaries">the first 12 miles from shore</a> are considered part of that country, but outside of that is international waters. </p>

<p>Though the Board on Geographic Names has changed the name to Gulf of America on official U.S. maps, and even if it approves the name change of Lake Ontario, there is no international board in charge of place names. Each country decides what to call places. And there is no official way for the U.S. to make other countries change the names on their maps. It’s possible, however, that the U.S. could formally ask other countries to change a name or even impose sanctions against countries that don’t comply.</p>

<p>Now that the names have been changed in the U.S., the government uses them in official documents, signage and maps. As for all the people and companies in the world that make maps, they usually use the official names. </p>

<p>Today, widely used online maps, including Google Maps, vary the display of place names based on the location from which you are viewing the map. If you view Google Maps from the U.S., you will see the name Gulf of America displayed; from Mexico, you will see the more traditional Gulf of Mexico. </p>

<p>Google and other mapping companies also do this with disputed borders. In fact, you can manually adjust your settings to show the map as if you were viewing it from another country. </p>
